yes_case.case: The closest historical episodes are the 2017 decision to exempt priority sector lending certificates (PSLC) from GST and the 2022 decision to impose 18% GST on corporate guarantees provided by holding companies to subsidiaries. This current episode differs crucially from the 2017 PSLC exemption because the modern co-lending architecture involves complex pass-through and assignment models rather than simple regulatory trading certificates, creating a massive perceived tax arbitrage opportunity for NBFC-bank partnerships that the fiscal authorities are eager to close. Furthermore, unlike the corporate guarantee ruling of 2022 which primarily targeted corporate balance sheet structuring, the NBFC-to-bank service fees directly touch retail credit intermediation margins, making it a high-yield revenue target that aligns with previous aggressive Council rulings on financial intermediary services.

In both past episodes, the Council faced strong industry resistance regarding cascading taxation on financial intermediation and ultimately delayed or heavily diluted implementation to protect credit flow. This episode differs fundamentally because NBFC-to-bank co-lending is a core systemic driver of current retail credit expansion, making the immediate implementation of an 18% levy far more disruptive to systemic liquidity than PSLCs or corporate guarantees ever were. Consequently, the Council will likely defer or reject the proposal to avoid tightening credit conditions.

yes_case.case: The primary structural friction in Indian fiscal federalism is the requirement of consensus or a three-fourths majority within the GST Council, which balances the power of the central government and the states. However, when revenue leakage or classification loopholes are identified—such as distinguishing between exempt financial services and taxable intermediary services provided by NBFCs to banks—the institutional machinery of the Law Committee and the Fitment Committee possesses a well-documented track record of processing clarifications and rate adjustments. Historically, once a revenue-generating harmonization proposal reaches the GST Council agenda with Fitment Committee backing, procedural friction is routinely overcome because states are incentivized to capture untapped tax bases. Frictions involving bureaucratic inertia or state-level dissent succeed in permanently blocking an agenda item in fewer than 15% of cases where the Centre actively pushes a standardized financial sector clarification. Therefore, structural friction is insufficient to prevent the formal Council approval before the deadline.

Historical precedent shows that fiscal harmonization proposals backed by the Centre successfully clear the Council's voting thresholds in the vast majority of instances.
